newsitem.title: Tajikistan: Red Cross suspends work in Tajikistan over kidnaps.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross suspends work in Tajikistan over kidnaps.

text.p: The Red Cross said on Thursday it had suspended operations in Tajikistan and sent all non-essential staff to neighbouring Uzbekistan after four United Nations workers were seized in the capital Dushanbe.

The Red Cross retreat responded to Thursday's kidnapping of four employees with the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR by assailants believed to have also seized up to 12 others in the remote Central Asian state.
In Geneva, Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, condemned the kidnappings and urged the Tajik government "to do its utmost" to secure their release.

"We deplore the kidnappings in the strongest possible terms," Ogata said in a statement. "The incident regrettably indicates the serious deterioration in the security situation for UNHCR and other international workers."

The UNHCR said the agency had had no contact with its four representatives -- an expatriate from Nigeria, a Tajik security guard and two Tajik drivers -- since they went missing in the centre of the capital with two marked U.N. cars.

But U.N. military observers in Tajikistan said the four were captured by the same armed rebel group that seized four U.N. military observers from Austria, Switzerland and Ukraine, two Red Cross workers and four Russian journalists.
The UNHCR figures differed slightly, putting the number of kidnapped military observers at five and the number of journalists who had been seized at five.
Ogata said all the hostages had been taken to Obigarm, 80 km (50 miles) east of Dushanbe, and called it "a stronghold of an armed opposition group believed reponsible for the kidnappings".
The Russian news agency Itar-Tass said it had received a telephone call from one of the kidnapped reporters, Galina Gridneva, who said their captors had told them they would be released on Friday.
The others would be freed only if the rebel group won safe passage back into the republic for comrades based in neighbouring Afghanistan, Tass quoted Gridneva as saying.
Both the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) said they had stopped work in the former Soviet republic bordering China.
"We have sent all non-essential staff out of the country," said Suzanne Berger, Geneva-based spokeswoman for the ICRC.
"There's no other way out, most of our operations are in the Garm valley," she said. "To send convoys there would be impossible."
The Two ICRC members held hostage were British national Elizabeth Trinch and her Tajik translator.
An official with the IFRC in Kazakhstan told Reuters the organisation had also suspended operations and moved all non-essential staff to Uzbekistan.

The agencies are based in the region to provide aid to the 5.7 million residents suffering hardship brought about by a bitter four-year civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and made many more homeless.
A ceasefire agreed between the government and the guerrillas has held for nearly two months and further peace talks are due to be held on February 26 in Moscow.
The latest hostage-taking was a setback for Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, who vowed to work for the hostages' release.
The hostage-takers are part of a group commanded by Rizyon Sadirov, who used to fight for Tajikstan's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.
"The president held an urgent meeting of the government this morning," presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov said. "He gave them the task of freeing hostages today by peaceful means.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said on Thursday the Kremlin leader was concerned by the hostage-taking and expected all Russian agencies to do "the maximum possible" to ensure the journalists were freed.
